question: The Planning Commission of India was set up in which year, and by what instrument?
option_1: In 1950, by an executive resolution of the Government of India
option_2: In 1947, by a resolution of the Constituent Assembly
option_3: In 1951, by an Act of Parliament
solution_text:
The correct answer is In 1950, by an executive resolution of the Government of India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Planning Commission was set up on 15 March 1950 by a simple executive resolution of the Government of India. (योजना आयोग — 15 मार्च 1950, कार्यपालिका संकल्प द्वारा)

 

• This is the point the question turns on. The Commission was:

 

• NOT a constitutional body — it finds no mention in the Constitution

 

• NOT a statutory body — it was not created by any Act of Parliament

 

• It was therefore an extra-constitutional and non-statutory advisory body, which is why it could be abolished as easily as it had been created.

 

• The Prime Minister was its ex-officio Chairman, and it had a Deputy Chairman of cabinet rank who ran it in practice. The first Deputy Chairman was Gulzarilal Nanda.

 

• It was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015 — again by an executive resolution.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The National Development Council (NDC), set up in 1952, was likewise created by an executive resolution. It included the Prime Minister, the Union ministers, the Chief Ministers of all states and the members of the Planning Commission, and it gave final approval to each Five Year Plan.

 

• The Finance Commission, by contrast, is a constitutional body, established under Article 280, and is appointed by the President every five years.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 (1947, Constituent Assembly): The Constituent Assembly framed the Constitution; it did not create the Planning Commission. An Advisory Planning Board was set up in 1946 under K.C. Neogy, but that is a different body.

 

• Option 3 (1951, Act of Parliament): 1951 was the year the First Five Year Plan was presented — but the Commission itself is not statutory, and this is the commonest misconception about it.

 

• Option 4 (1952, Constitutional Amendment): 1952 was the year of the National Development Council, and no constitutional amendment was involved in either body.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.
II. NITI Aayog, like the Planning Commission before it, has the power to allocate funds to the states.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only I.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog — the National Institution for Transforming India — on 1 January 2015. (नीति आयोग — 1 जनवरी 2015)

 

• Statement II is INCORRECT. NITI Aayog has NO power to allocate funds to the states.

 

• The Planning Commission did allocate plan funds, and this gave it real authority over the states.

 

• NITI Aayog is a think tank and advisory body only. The allocation of funds now rests with the Ministry of Finance.

 

• NITI Aayog's stated approach is "cooperative and competitive federalism" — the states are meant to be partners in framing policy rather than recipients of a plan handed down from Delhi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The structure of NITI Aayog:

 

• Chairperson – the Prime Minister

 

• Vice-Chairperson – appointed by the Prime Minister; the first was Arvind Panagariya

 

• Governing Council – the Chief Ministers of all states and the Lieutenant Governors of the union territories

 

• CEO – an officer of the rank of Secretary to the Government of India

 

• Its published work includes the SDG India Index, the National Multidimensional Poverty Index, and the indices for health, education and water management.

 

NOTE

 

• Since Statement I is correct and Statement II is not, Option 2 (Only II), Option 3 (Both I and II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• Statement II is the standard trap. Candidates assume that a body which replaces another inherits its powers — but the loss of the power to allocate funds is precisely the difference between the two institutions.

question: The Lingayat or Virashaiva movement of Karnataka was founded by _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Basavanna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Lingayat or Virashaiva movement was founded in the twelfth century by Basavanna (also called Basaveshwara), a minister at the court of the Kalachuri king Bijjala at Kalyana in Karnataka. (लिंगायत आंदोलन — बसवन्ना)

 

• Its principal features were:

 

• Devotion to Shiva in the form of the Ishtalinga, worn on the person

 

• A firm rejection of caste, of image worship in temples, of ritual and of the authority of the Vedas

 

• The rejection of child marriage, and support for widow remarriage

 

• Burial of the dead in place of cremation

 

• Its teachings were composed in Kannada prose-poems called Vachanas, written in the language of the people rather than in Sanskrit — which is why the movement reached so far beyond the learned.

 

• Basavanna founded the Anubhava Mantapa, an assembly at which men and women of every caste debated religious and social questions on equal terms.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Lingayat movement is one of the earliest and most radical of the Bhakti movements in its social teaching, and its refusal of caste distinctions went further than most.

 

• Its followers are also known as Lingayats because of the linga worn about the neck, and they remain a substantial community in Karnataka and the neighbouring states.

 

NOTE

 

• Allama Prabhu (Option 1): A great mystic of the same movement and the presiding figure of the Anubhava Mantapa, but not its founder. He is the closest distractor here.

 

• Akka Mahadevi (Option 2): The most celebrated woman saint of the movement, whose Vachanas are among the finest in Kannada literature. She was a contemporary of Basavanna, not the founder.

 

• Purandara Dasa (Option 4): A Haridasa saint of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and a Vaishnavite. He is regarded as the father of Carnatic music — a different tradition and a later age altogether.

question: In the human digestive system, most of the water from the undigested food is absorbed in the _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is large intestine.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The LARGE INTESTINE absorbs most of the water from the undigested food that reaches it, converting the liquid residue into semi-solid faeces. (बड़ी आंत — जल का अवशोषण)

 

• It absorbs no nutrients of consequence; its work is the recovery of water and of some mineral salts.

 

• It is about 1.5 metres long and consists of the caecum, the colon and the rectum.

 

• Two disorders follow directly from its working, and both are commonly examined:

 

• If water is absorbed too slowly, the result is diarrhoea

 

• If it is absorbed too thoroughly, the result is constipation

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The digestive tract and what happens where:

 

• Mouth – chewing; salivary amylase begins the digestion of starch

 

• Oesophagus – conducts food by peristalsis; no digestion

 

• Stomach – pepsin digests protein in an acid medium (HCl); some water and alcohol absorbed

 

• Small intestine – most digestion is completed and most nutrients absorbed, through the villi. It is about 6 metres long, the longest part of the tract

 

• Large intestine – absorption of water

 

• The liver secretes bile, and the pancreas the pancreatic juice; both empty into the small intestine.

 

NOTE

 

• stomach (Option 1): Some water and alcohol are absorbed here, but the stomach's principal work is the digestion of protein, not the recovery of water.

 

• small intestine (Option 2): The strongest distractor, since it absorbs most of the nutrients and is where digestion is completed. But the water left in the residue is taken up further along, in the large intestine.

 

• oesophagus (Option 4): A muscular tube that merely conveys food from the throat to the stomach. Neither digestion nor absorption takes place in it.

question: In the absence of oxygen, the breakdown of pyruvate in human muscle cells produces _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is lactic acid.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When oxygen is scarce, as during vigorous exercise, the pyruvate produced by glycolysis is broken down in the muscle cells into LACTIC ACID. (लैक्टिक अम्ल — अवायवीय श्वसन)

 

• This is anaerobic respiration, and it takes place in the cytoplasm, not in the mitochondria.

 

• The accumulation of lactic acid in the muscles causes cramps and the aching that follows hard exercise. It is cleared once the supply of oxygen is restored, which is why the ache is relieved by rest and by massage, both of which improve the blood flow.

 

• Anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per molecule of glucose, against the 36 to 38 ATP of aerobic respiration — which is why it can sustain effort only briefly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three fates of pyruvate:

 

• With oxygen (aerobic) — broken down in the mitochondria to carbon dioxide and water, releasing much energy

 

• Without oxygen, in muscle — converted to lactic acid

 

• Without oxygen, in yeast — converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide. This is fermentation, and is the basis of brewing and of the rising of bread

 

• Glycolysis, the first stage common to all three, always takes place in the cytoplasm and splits one glucose molecule into two of pyruvate.

 

NOTE

 

• ethanol and carbon dioxide (Option 2): The products of anaerobic respiration in YEAST, not in human muscle. This is the principal trap, since both are anaerobic pathways from the same starting point.

 

• acetic acid (Option 3): The acid of vinegar, produced by the bacterial oxidation of ethanol — a different process altogether.

 

• glucose and water (Option 4): Glucose is the starting material of respiration, not a product of it.

question: The "Purusha Sukta", which contains the earliest reference to the four varnas, is found in which Mandala of the Rigveda?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tenth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Purusha Sukta is hymn 90 of the TENTH MANDALA of the Rigveda, and contains the earliest mention of the four varnas — Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra. (पुरुष सूक्त — ऋग्वेद का दसवाँ मंडल)

 

• It describes the four as having arisen from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet of the cosmic being Purusha.

 

• Its position matters historically. The first and tenth Mandalas are the latest portions of the Rigveda, added after the rest; Mandalas two to seven are the oldest and are called the family books, each ascribed to a particular clan of seers.

 

• The mention of varna in the latest layer of the text is therefore taken as evidence that the fourfold division was a late development in the Vedic period, not an original feature of it.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Rigveda in brief:

 

• 10 Mandalas, 1,028 hymns (suktas), about 10,600 verses

 

• Mandalas 2-7 – the oldest, the family books

 

• Mandala 9 – devoted entirely to Soma, the deity of the sacred plant

 

• Mandala 3 – contains the Gayatri Mantra, addressed to Savitri and composed by Vishvamitra

 

• Mandala 10 – the Purusha Sukta, the Nasadiya Sukta (the hymn of creation) and the dialogue hymns

 

• The Rigveda was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.

 

NOTE

 

• First Mandala (Option 1): The other late addition to the collection, and the longest. It is the strongest distractor, since the first and tenth are of the same period.

 

• Seventh Mandala (Option 2): One of the family books, ascribed to Vasishtha, and containing the account of the Battle of the Ten Kings (Dasarajna).

 

• Ninth Mandala (Option 3): Devoted wholly to the Soma Pavamana hymns, and unique in being addressed to a single deity throughout.

question: "Bardo Chham", the mask dance performed by the Sherdukpen community, belongs to which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arunachal Pradesh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Bardo Chham is a mask dance of the Sherdukpen community of ARUNACHAL PRADESH, performed chiefly in the West Kameng district. (बार्दो छम — अरुणाचल प्रदेश)

 

• Its subject is the struggle between good and evil. The Sherdukpens hold that mankind faces twelve evil forces, appearing in different forms in each month of the year, and the dancers wear masks of animals representing those forces.

 

• It is performed over several days in January and in September, to the beat of drums and cymbals, and ends with the symbolic defeat of the evil spirits.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other dances of Arunachal Pradesh: Ponung and Popir (of the Adi and Galo), Rikham Pada (of the Nyishi), Wancho dance, Chalo (of the Nocte) and the Buddhist Aji Lhamu of the Monpas.

 

• Arunachal Pradesh has 26 major tribes and over 100 sub-tribes, and is the most linguistically diverse state in India. It became a full state on 20 February 1987, and its capital is Itanagar.

 

NOTE

 

• Sikkim (Option 1): Known for the Singhi Chham (the snow-lion dance), Yak Chham, Maruni and the monastic Chaam performed at Losoong.

 

• Mizoram (Option 2): Known for Cheraw (the bamboo dance), Khuallam, Chheihlam and Sarlamkai.

 

• Nagaland (Option 3): Known for the Zeliang, Chang Lo (Sua Lua) and Modse dances, performed above all at the Hornbill Festival.

question: The "Dhalo" and "Fugdi" dances, performed by women, belong to which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Goa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Dhalo and Fugdi are traditional folk dances of GOA, both performed exclusively by women. (धालो एवं फुगड़ी — गोवा)

 

• DHALO is a ritual dance performed over several nights in the month of Pausha (January), in which women stand in two facing rows, arms linked, and sing invocations for the prosperity of their families. It is regarded as a prayer for the protection of the household.

 

• FUGDI is danced during Ganesh Chaturthi and the month of Bhadrapada, in circles or rows, and begins slowly before working up to a very rapid tempo. Its name comes from the sound of the dancers' heavy breathing at the close.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other folk forms of Goa: Dekhni (a half-Hindu, half-Christian dance form), Mando (a slow song-and-dance of the Goan Catholic community), Ghode Modni (a dummy-horse warrior dance), Talgadi, Kunbi and the Shigmo spring festival.

 

• Goa became the 25th state of India on 30 May 1987, having been a union territory since its liberation from Portuguese rule in 1961. Its capital is Panaji.

 

NOTE

 

• Maharashtra (Option 1): The strongest distractor, since Goa's culture is closely related to the Konkan coast of Maharashtra. Maharashtra's own forms are Lavani, Tamasha, Powada, Dindi and Gondhal.

 

• Karnataka (Option 3): Known for Yakshagana, Dollu Kunitha, Veeragase and Bhootha Aradhane.

 

• Gujarat (Option 4): Known for Garba, Dandiya Raas, Tippani and Padhar.

question: Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Manipur.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Keibul Lamjao National Park lies in the Bishnupur district of MANIPUR, on Loktak Lake, and is the only floating national park in the world. (केइबुल लामजाओ — मणिपुर)

 

• It floats because it rests on phumdis — thick mats of vegetation, soil and organic matter in various stages of decomposition, which drift on the surface of the lake. About four-fifths of the park is made of them.

 

• It was created to protect the Sangai, the brow-antlered deer of Manipur, also called the dancing deer for its peculiar gait as it steps across the yielding phumdis. The Sangai is the state animal of Manipur and is found nowhere else in the world.

 

• The area was declared a sanctuary in 1966 and a National Park in 1977.

 

• Loktak Lake, on which it stands, is the largest freshwater lake in north-eastern India and a Ramsar site. It has been placed on the Montreux Record, the list of Ramsar sites where ecological change has occurred.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sangai was believed to be extinct in 1951, and was rediscovered soon afterwards. Its numbers, once down to about fourteen, have since recovered slowly but it remains endangered.

 

NOTE

 

• Assam (Option 2): Its national parks are Kaziranga (the one-horned rhinoceros), Manas, Nameri, Orang and Dibru-Saikhowa — the first two being World Heritage Sites.

 

• Tripura (Option 3): Known for the Clouded Leopard National Park and the Sepahijala and Trishna wildlife sanctuaries.

 

• Meghalaya (Option 4): Known for the Nokrek and Balpakram national parks; Nokrek is a biosphere reserve famous for the wild citrus *Citrus indica*.

question: "Tusu Parab", the harvest festival marked by the immersion of decorated wooden frames, is celebrated chiefly in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jharkhand.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tusu Parab, also called Makar Parab, is a harvest festival of JHARKHAND, celebrated also in the neighbouring districts of West Bengal and Odisha. (टुसू पर्व — झारखंड)

 

• It is held at the end of the month of Poush, around Makar Sankranti in mid-January, when the winter harvest is gathered.

 

• Its distinguishing feature is the Tusu — a decorated wooden or bamboo frame, brightly ornamented with coloured paper — which unmarried girls carry in procession and then immerse in a river or tank at the close of the festival.

 

• The songs sung during it are called Tusu geet, and are composed and sung by women.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other festivals of Jharkhand: Sarhul (the festival of the sal tree, marking the new year for the Oraon and Munda), Karma (in which a branch of the karam tree is worshipped), Sohrai (the cattle festival of the Santhals) and Bandna.

 

• Jharkhand was created on 15 November 2000, the birth anniversary of Birsa Munda, as the 28th state of India. Its capital is Ranchi.

 

NOTE

 

• Bihar (Option 1): Known for Chhath Puja, the Sonepur Fair, Sama Chakeva and the Pitrapaksha Mela at Gaya.

 

• Odisha (Option 3): Tusu is observed in its western districts, which makes this a genuine distractor — but the festival's home is Jharkhand. Odisha's own festivals are the Rath Yatra, Nuakhai and Raja Parba.

 

• Assam (Option 4): Its harvest festival is Magh Bihu (Bhogali Bihu), celebrated at the same season in January but with feasting and bonfires rather than immersion.

question: The "Ka Pomblang Nongkrem" festival, held at Smit, is celebrated by which community of Meghalaya?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Khasis.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ka Pomblang Nongkrem, usually shortened to the Nongkrem Dance, is the great festival of the KHASI community of Meghalaya. (नोंगक्रेम — खासी समुदाय)

 

• It is held over five days in October or November at Smit, the traditional seat of the Syiem of Khyrim, the Khasi chief.

 

• It is a thanksgiving for the harvest and a prayer for peace and prosperity, offered to the goddess Ka Blei Synshar.

 

• Its central rite is the Pomblang, the sacrifice of goats, performed by the Syiem and the high priest. Unmarried girls in gold and silver ornaments dance within an enclosure while the men dance around them with swords and whisks.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Meghalaya has three principal communities, and each has its own festivals:

 

• Khasi – Ka Pomblang Nongkrem, Shad Suk Mynsiem (the dance of the joyful heart, in April)

 

• Garo – Wangala, the hundred-drums harvest festival held in November

 

• Jaintia – Behdienkhlam, held in July to drive away plague and disease

 

• All three communities are matrilineal — descent and inheritance pass through the mother, and the youngest daughter inherits the ancestral property.

 

NOTE

 

• Garos (Option 1): Their harvest festival is Wangala, celebrated in honour of the sun god Misi Saljong, and famous for the simultaneous beating of a hundred drums.

 

• Jaintias (Option 2): Their festival is Behdienkhlam, held at Jowai, in which decorated wooden structures are carried and a wooden post is used in a ritual tug of war.

 

• Hajongs (Option 4): A smaller community found in Meghalaya and Assam, whose festivals are Bishua and Pushna. They are not associated with Nongkrem.

question: In which year was the Sikh kingdom of Punjab finally annexed by the British?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1849.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sikh kingdom of Punjab was annexed by the British in 1849, at the end of the Second Anglo-Sikh War. (पंजाब का विलय — 1849)

 

• The annexation was carried out by Lord Dalhousie, and Punjab was the last major territory to be added to British India.

 

• The young Maharaja Duleep Singh was deposed and sent to England, and the Koh-i-Noor diamond was surrendered to the British Crown.

 

• Punjab was placed under a Board of Administration, of which John Lawrence and Henry Lawrence were members.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The sequence in Punjab:

 

• 1839 – death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, followed by ten years of disorder at Lahore

 

• 1845-46 – First Anglo-Sikh War, ending in the Treaty of Lahore (1846), by which the Sikhs ceded the Jalandhar Doab and paid an indemnity

 

• 1846 – the Treaty of Bhairowal, placing Punjab under a British Resident

 

• 1848-49 – Second Anglo-Sikh War; the battles of Chillianwala and Gujrat

 

• 1849 – annexation

 

• Punjab's loyalty to the British during the Revolt of 1857 — only eight years after annexation — was a decisive factor in the recapture of Delhi.

 

NOTE

 

• 1839 (Option 1): The year of Ranjit Singh's death. The kingdom survived him by ten years, and this is the commonest wrong answer.

 

• 1846 (Option 2): The year of the Treaty of Lahore, which ended the First Anglo-Sikh War. Punjab lost territory and independence of action but was not annexed.

 

• 1857 (Option 4): The year of the Revolt, eight years after the annexation was complete.

question: A geostationary satellite is placed in an orbit at what approximate height above the earth's equator?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 36,000 km.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A geostationary satellite orbits at a height of about 36,000 km above the earth's equator. (भूस्थिर उपग्रह — लगभग 36,000 किमी)

 

• Three conditions must all be satisfied for a satellite to appear stationary from the ground:

 

• Its orbital period must be 24 hours, matching the earth's rotation

 

• It must orbit directly above the equator, in the equatorial plane

 

• It must move west to east, in the same direction as the earth's rotation

 

• Only one height gives a period of exactly 24 hours, and that height is about 35,786 km, usually rounded to 36,000 km.

 

• Because such a satellite appears fixed in the sky, a dish antenna pointed at it never has to be moved — which is what makes communication and television broadcasting possible.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Types of satellite orbit:

 

• Geostationary (GEO) – about 36,000 km; used for communication, broadcasting and weather. India's INSAT and GSAT series.

 

• Polar / Sun-synchronous – about 800-900 km; passes over the poles and covers the whole earth strip by strip. Used for remote sensing. India's IRS, Cartosat and Resourcesat.

 

• Low Earth Orbit (LEO) – 200 to 2,000 km; the International Space Station orbits at about 400 km.

 

• Three geostationary satellites, spaced 120° apart, can cover almost the whole surface of the earth.

 

NOTE

 

• 3,600 km (Option 1): A tenth of the correct height — the trap being a misplaced decimal. At this height a satellite would circle the earth in about three hours.

 

• 3,60,000 km (Option 3): Ten times the correct height, and close to the distance of the Moon (about 3,84,000 km).

 

• 1,000 km (Option 4): The region of low earth orbit, used by remote-sensing satellites, which complete a revolution in about 100 minutes.

question: The recoil of a gun when it is fired is an illustration of _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Newton’s third law of motion.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The recoil of a gun illustrates Newton's THIRD law of motion: *to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction*. (न्यूटन का तृतीय गति नियम)

 

• The gun exerts a forward force on the bullet; the bullet exerts an equal and opposite backward force on the gun, which is felt as the recoil or kick.

 

• The two are equal in momentum, not in speed. Since the gun is far more massive than the bullet, it moves back far more slowly:

 

• m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ — a heavy gun therefore recoils gently, and a light one sharply.

 

• This also explains why a rifle is held firmly against the shoulder: the mass of the shooter is added to that of the rifle, and the recoil velocity falls further still.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other illustrations of the third law:

 

• The launching of a rocket — hot gases are driven downward, and the rocket rises

 

• Walking — the foot pushes the ground backward, and the ground pushes the walker forward

 

• The backward movement of a boat as a man steps forward from it onto the bank

 

• Swimming — the hands push the water backward, and the water pushes the swimmer forward

 

• The third law explains why forces always occur in pairs, and why the two never act on the same body — which is why they do not cancel each other out.

 

NOTE

 

• First law (Option 1): The law of inertia — a body continues at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by an external force. It explains why a passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

 

• Second law (Option 2): F = ma — the force equals the rate of change of momentum. It explains why a cricketer draws his hands back while catching a ball, and is genuinely involved in the recoil, but the pairing of forces is the third law's business.

 

• Law of universal gravitation (Option 4): Governs the attraction between two masses, and has nothing to do with recoil.

question: India's Mars Orbiter Mission, popularly called Mangalyaan, was launched in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2013.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), or Mangalyaan, was launched on 5 November 2013 from Sriharikota by the PSLV-C25, and entered Martian orbit on 24 September 2014. (मंगलयान — 2013)

 

• Three things make it remarkable, and all three are examined:

 

• India became the first country to reach Mars orbit at its first attempt

 

• India became the first Asian country to reach Mars

 

• It cost about Rs 450 crore — a fraction of the cost of comparable missions, and famously less than that of some feature films

 

• It was designed for a life of six months and continued to send data for about eight years, until 2022.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Milestones of the Indian space programme:

 

• 1975 – Aryabhata, the first Indian satellite

 

• 1980 – Rohini RS-1, on the indigenous SLV-3

 

• 2008 – Chandrayaan-1, which found evidence of water molecules on the Moon

 

• 2013 – Mangalyaan

 

• 2019 – Chandrayaan-2; the orbiter succeeded, the lander did not

 

• 2023 – Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole, a first for any country; and Aditya-L1 was launched to study the Sun

 

NOTE

 

• 2008 (Option 1): The year of Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar mission, whose Moon Impact Probe carried the Indian flag to the lunar surface.

 

• 2019 (Option 2): The year of Chandrayaan-2 and of Mission Shakti, India's anti-satellite test.

 

• 2017 (Option 3): The year in which ISRO launched 104 satellites in a single flight aboard the PSLV-C37 — a world record at the time.

question: In the Baul tradition of Bengal, the single-stringed instrument played by the singer is called the _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ektara.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The EKTARA is the single-stringed instrument of the Baul singers of Bengal. Its name says so — "ek" means one and "tara" a string. (एकतारा — एक तार)

 

• It is made from a gourd or a wooden bowl covered with skin, with a split bamboo neck; the player presses the two halves of the bamboo to change the tension of the string, and so the pitch.

 

• The Bauls are wandering mystic minstrels of Bengal, whose songs teach a devotion that rejects caste, ritual and religious division. The tradition was inscribed by UNESCO in 2005 as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

 

• Their music deeply influenced Rabindranath Tagore, and through him a good deal of modern Bengali song. Lalon Fakir is the most celebrated of the Baul composers.

 

• The Baul's usual equipment is the ektara in one hand, the duggi (a small drum) at the waist, and ghungroo at the ankles.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• A useful set of stringed instruments named by their number of strings: Ektara (one), Dotara (two), Sitar (from *seh-tar*, three strings in origin), Sarod, Santoor (a hundred strings) and Veena.

 

NOTE

 

• Dotara (Option 1): A two-stringed plucked instrument — in practice often four or five — used in the folk music of Bengal, Assam and Bihar. The strongest distractor, since it is played in the same region and often alongside the ektara.

 

• Sarinda (Option 3): A bowed instrument of Rajasthan, Assam and Tripura, carved from a single block of wood.

 

• Khamak (Option 4): A plucked drum, sometimes called the anandalahari, in which the string is attached to a drum head and pulled to vary the pitch. It is used by Bauls, but it is not the single-stringed instrument in question.

question: A solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at a given temperature is called _____.
solution_text:
The correct answer is a saturated solution.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A SATURATED SOLUTION is one in which no more solute can be dissolved at a given temperature. (संतृप्त विलयन)

 

• The words "at a given temperature" are essential, and are the whole difficulty of the definition. A solution saturated at 20°C is not saturated at 60°C, because solubility rises with temperature for most solids.

 

• The solubility of a substance is defined as the maximum quantity that will dissolve in 100 grams of solvent at a stated temperature.

 

• If more solute is added to a saturated solution, it simply settles at the bottom undissolved.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Types of solution by concentration:

 

• Unsaturated – more solute can still be dissolved

 

• Saturated – no more can be dissolved at that temperature

 

• Supersaturated – contains more dissolved solute than it should at that temperature; an unstable state, obtained by cooling a hot saturated solution slowly and without disturbance

 

• Note that for gases the rule reverses: the solubility of a gas in a liquid falls as the temperature rises, which is why a warm aerated drink goes flat quickly, and why fish are distressed in warm water.

 

NOTE

 

• a dilute solution (Option 2): One containing a small quantity of solute in relation to the solvent. Dilute and concentrated are relative terms; saturated is an exact one.

 

• a colloidal solution (Option 3): Not a true solution at all. Its particles are between 1 and 1000 nanometres, large enough to scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.

 

• a supersaturated solution (Option 4): The subtlest distractor. It holds more solute than a saturated solution, so it is not the answer — but it is unstable, and a single crystal dropped into it will make the excess crystallise out at once.

question: The Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva), India's largest container port, is located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT), also called Nhava Sheva, is in Navi Mumbai, MAHARASHTRA, on the Arabian Sea across the harbour from Mumbai Port. (जवाहरलाल नेहरू पोर्ट — महाराष्ट्र)

 

• It is India's largest container port, handling well over half the country's container traffic, and was commissioned in 1989.

 

• It was built to relieve the congestion at the old Mumbai Port, which could not handle modern container vessels.

 

• It is now formally named the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority (JNPA), following the Major Port Authorities Act, 2021.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The major ports of India, west coast to east:

 

• Deendayal (Kandla) – Gujarat; a tidal port

 

• Mumbai and Jawaharlal Nehru – Maharashtra

 

• Mormugao – Goa, known for iron ore exports

 

• New Mangalore – Karnataka; Cochin – Kerala

 

• V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin), Chennai, Kamarajar (Ennore) – Tamil Nadu

 

• Visakhapatnam – Andhra Pradesh, the deepest land-locked port

 

• Paradip – Odisha; Syama Prasad Mookerjee (Kolkata) – West Bengal, the only riverine major port

 

• Vizhinjam in Kerala is India's first deep-water transhipment port.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): Has the longest coastline of any Indian state, and the major port of Deendayal (Kandla), besides the large private port at Mundra. It is the strongest distractor on sheer volume of traffic.

 

• Goa (Option 3): Site of Mormugao, a natural harbour developed chiefly for the export of iron ore from the Western Ghats.

 

• Karnataka (Option 4): Site of New Mangalore, which handles iron ore, petroleum products and fertilisers.

question: Which of the following activities belongs to the secondary sector of the economy?
option_1: Weaving cloth in a textile mill
solution_text:
The correct answer is Weaving cloth in a textile mill.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The SECONDARY SECTOR covers activities in which a natural product is transformed into another form through manufacturing. Weaving cotton into cloth is exactly such a transformation. (द्वितीयक क्षेत्र — विनिर्माण)

 

• The three sectors, and the test for each:

 

• PRIMARY – produces goods by exploiting nature directly: agriculture, fishing, mining, forestry, dairying. Also called the *agriculture and allied* sector.

 

• SECONDARY – manufactures and processes: mills, factories, construction, generation of electricity. Also called the *industrial* sector.

 

• TERTIARY – provides services that support the other two: transport, banking, insurance, trade, education, health, administration. Also called the *service* sector.

 

• The test to apply is a single question: is a natural product being extracted, transformed, or served?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• In India's economy the tertiary sector contributes the largest share of GDP — well over half — while the primary sector still employs the largest number of people. This mismatch between output and employment is the central structural feature of the Indian economy.

 

• India is unusual in having moved from a largely primary economy to a largely service economy without passing through a long phase of manufacturing dominance.

 

NOTE

 

• Catching fish (Option 2): PRIMARY — a natural product is being taken directly from nature, with no transformation.

 

• Teaching in a school (Option 3): TERTIARY — a service. Nothing material is produced.

 

• Transporting goods by road (Option 4): TERTIARY — transport is a service that supports production and trade, and does not itself make anything. This is the strongest distractor, since it is closely tied to industry.

question: Which body is the regulator of the pension sector in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is PFRDA.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is the regulator of the pension sector in India. (पेंशन निधि विनियामक एवं विकास प्राधिकरण)

 

• It was established in 2003 and given statutory status by the PFRDA Act, 2013. Its headquarters is at New Delhi.

 

• It regulates the National Pension System (NPS) and the Atal Pension Yojana (APY).

 

• The NPS was made compulsory for central government employees joining service on or after 1 January 2004, and was opened to all citizens in 2009.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's principal financial regulators — a set worth memorising:

 

• RBI (1935) – banking, currency and monetary policy; Mumbai

 

• SEBI (1988; statutory 1992) – the securities market; Mumbai

 

• IRDAI (1999) – insurance; Hyderabad

 

• PFRDA (2003; statutory 2013) – pensions; New Delhi

 

• NABARD (1982) – agricultural and rural credit; Mumbai

 

• IBBI (2016) – insolvency and bankruptcy; New Delhi

 

• FSDC, chaired by the Union Finance Minister, is the apex body coordinating all of them.

 

NOTE

 

• SEBI (Option 1): The Securities and Exchange Board of India, which regulates the stock exchanges, mutual funds and the protection of investors — not pensions.

 

• IRDAI (Option 3): The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, set up on the recommendation of the Malhotra Committee. It regulates life and general insurance. It is the strongest distractor, since pension products are often sold by insurers.

 

• NABARD (Option 4): The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development, set up on the recommendation of the Sivaraman Committee, which refinances rural credit.

question: Which of the following books was written by Ruskin Bond?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Room on the Roof.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Room on the Roof" was written by Ruskin Bond, and published in 1956. (द रूम ऑन द रूफ — रस्किन बॉन्ड)

 

• He wrote it at the age of seventeen, and it won the John Llewellyn Rhys Prize in 1957 — an award for a British Commonwealth writer under thirty.

 

• It tells the story of Rusty, an Anglo-Indian orphan in Dehradun who runs away from his English guardian to live among Indian friends. Its sequel is "Vagrants in the Valley".

 

• Bond's other well-known works include "The Blue Umbrella", "A Flight of Pigeons" (filmed as *Junoon*), "Rusty" series, "Time Stops at Shamli" and "Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra", which won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1992.

 

• He received the Padma Shri in 1999 and the Padma Bhushan in 2014.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ruskin Bond has lived at Landour, near Mussoorie, for most of his life, and the Himalayan foothills are the setting of nearly everything he has written.

 

NOTE

 

• Train to Pakistan (Option 2): Written by Khushwant Singh (1956), the classic novel of Partition, set in the fictional village of Mano Majra on the border.

 

• A House for Mr Biswas (Option 3): Written by V.S. Naipaul (1961), the Trinidad-born writer of Indian descent who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2001.

 

• The Shadow Lines (Option 4): Written by Amitav Ghosh (1988), which won the Sahitya Akademi Award. Ghosh was the first writer in English to receive the Jnanpith Award, in 2018.

question: Who wrote "Gita Rahasya" during his imprisonment at Mandalay?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bal Gangadhar Tilak.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Gita Rahasya", properly *Shrimad Bhagavadgita Rahasya*, was written by Bal Gangadhar Tilak during his imprisonment at Mandalay in Burma, where he was held from 1908 to 1914. (गीता रहस्य — बाल गंगाधर तिलक)

 

• He had been sentenced to six years' transportation for sedition, for his writings in Kesari defending the revolutionaries.

 

• The book's argument is that the Bhagavad Gita teaches Karma Yoga — the path of action — and not renunciation. Tilak read it as a call to active work in the world, and so as a religious sanction for political struggle.

 

• Tilak is remembered for the declaration "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it." He was called "Lokmanya", and Valentine Chirol described him as "the Father of Indian Unrest".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tilak founded the newspapers Kesari (in Marathi) and Maratha (in English), and revived the Ganapati and Shivaji festivals as instruments of public mobilisation.

 

• With Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal he formed the "Lal-Bal-Pal" trio of Extremist leaders. He founded the Home Rule League in 1916 at Pune, in the same year as Annie Besant's League.

 

NOTE

 

• Aurobindo Ghosh (Option 1): Tried in the Alipore Bomb Case (1908) and acquitted, after which he withdrew to Pondicherry. He wrote "The Life Divine", "Savitri" and "Essays on the Gita" — the last of which makes him the closest distractor here.

 

• Lala Lajpat Rai (Option 3): Called "Punjab Kesari", author of "Unhappy India" and "Young India", and deported to Mandalay in 1907 — a year before Tilak, which is a further reason this option is placed here.

 

• Bipin Chandra Pal (Option 4): The third of the trio, a journalist and orator, author of "The New Spirit" and "Memories of My Life and Times".

question: Which of the following is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Santiniketan, West Bengal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Santiniketan, in the Birbhum district of West Bengal, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in September 2023. (शांतिनिकेतन — यूनेस्को विश्व धरोहर, 2023)

 

• It was founded as an ashram by Debendranath Tagore in 1863, and developed by his son Rabindranath Tagore, who established a school there in 1901 and the university Visva-Bharati in 1921.

 

• Its educational ideal was teaching in the open air, under the trees, and the blending of the best of Indian and Western learning — expressed in the university's motto, *Yatra Visvam Bhavatyekanidam*, "where the world makes a home in a single nest".

 

• Santiniketan is a cultural site, and was the first inscription in India of a place valued primarily for a living educational and artistic tradition rather than for its architecture alone.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• India has 44 World Heritage Sites. Recent inscriptions: Dholavira (2021), Santiniketan (2023), the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (2023), Moidams of Assam (2024) and the Maratha Military Landscapes (2025).

 

• The first Indian sites, all inscribed in 1983, were Ajanta, Ellora, Agra Fort and the Taj Mahal.

 

NOTE

 

• Kamakhya Temple (Option 1): A major Shakti Peetha at Guwahati, and the site of the Ambubachi Mela — but not on the UNESCO list. Assam's World Heritage Sites are Kaziranga, Manas and the Moidams.

 

• Akshardham Temple, New Delhi (Option 2): Completed in 2005. A World Heritage Site must ordinarily be of outstanding value established over time, and a building two decades old does not qualify.

 

• Golden Temple, Amritsar (Option 3): The Harmandir Sahib, the most visited religious building in India. It stands on India's tentative list but has not been inscribed.

question: The Jantar Mantar inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site is located in which city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jaipur.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Jantar Mantar at JAIPUR was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010. (जंतर मंतर, जयपुर — यूनेस्को विश्व धरोहर)

 

• It was built between 1727 and 1734 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, who built five such observatories in all — at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi.

 

• The Jaipur observatory is the largest and best preserved of the five, and is the only one inscribed by UNESCO.

 

• It contains nineteen instruments built of stone and marble, of which the greatest is the Samrat Yantra, a sundial 27 metres high that tells the local time to an accuracy of about two seconds.

 

• Other instruments include the Jai Prakash Yantra, the Ram Yantra and the Rashivalaya Yantra, which has twelve parts, one for each sign of the zodiac.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The word "Jantar Mantar" derives from *yantra* (instrument) and *mantra* (formula or calculation).

 

• Sawai Jai Singh II also founded the city of Jaipur in 1727, laid out on a grid by the architect Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. The walled city of Jaipur was itself inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2019.

 

NOTE

 

• New Delhi (Option 2): Also has a Jantar Mantar, built in 1724 and the first of the five — which makes it the strongest distractor. It is smaller, more damaged by the growth of the city around it, and is not on the UNESCO list.

 

• Ujjain (Option 3): Has an observatory built by the same ruler. Ujjain has an ancient association with astronomy, since the prime meridian of Indian astronomy was traditionally taken to pass through it.

 

• Varanasi (Option 4): Its observatory stands on the roof of the Man Mandir Ghat palace, overlooking the Ganga.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

I. An electric fuse works on the heating effect of electric current.
II. A moving coil galvanometer works on the magnetic effect of electric current.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement I is CORRECT. An electric fuse works on the HEATING EFFECT of electric current. (विद्युत फ्यूज — धारा का ऊष्मीय प्रभाव)

 

• A fuse is a short piece of wire of high resistance and low melting point, usually an alloy of tin and lead.

 

• When the current exceeds a safe value, the heat produced — given by H = I²Rt, Joule's law — melts the wire and breaks the circuit.

 

• A fuse is always connected in the live wire and in series with the appliance.

 

• Statement II is CORRECT. A moving coil galvanometer works on the MAGNETIC EFFECT of electric current.

 

• A current-carrying coil suspended in a magnetic field experiences a torque and rotates, and the deflection is proportional to the current.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three effects of electric current, and their applications:

 

• HEATING effect – electric fuse, electric iron, heater, geyser, incandescent bulb, toaster

 

• MAGNETIC effect – electric motor, generator, galvanometer, electric bell, loudspeaker, electromagnet, MRI

 

• CHEMICAL effect – electroplating, electrolysis, the extraction of metals, electric cells

 

• A galvanometer detects and measures small currents. Converted with a high resistance in series it becomes a voltmeter; with a low resistance in parallel (a shunt) it becomes an ammeter.

 

NOTE

 

• Since both statements are correct, Option 1 (Only I), Option 2 (Only II) and Option 4 (Neither I nor II) are all ruled out.

 

• The commonest error in questions of this kind is to attribute the fuse to the magnetic effect, by association with the circuit-breaker — which does indeed work magnetically. The fuse melts; the circuit-breaker trips.
